name: Averroes on reason, revelation, and the unity of intellect
plain_explanation: Averroes argued two things that got him into trouble with the pious: first, that reason alone (without revelation) can prove God exists; and second, following Aristotle, that while the individual soul is not immortal, 'intellect' (nous) is immortal -- but since intellect is one and the same in all people, this does not give any individual person personal survival after death.
precise_definition: The position that (a) God's existence is a truth demonstrable by unaided natural reason, and (b) what survives death is an impersonal, universal intellect rather than an individuated personal soul, since intellect is numerically one across all thinking beings.
why_it_mattered: It directly denied personal immortality, a doctrine central to popular religion, and so became the flashpoint for the 'Averroist' controversy that convulsed the University of Paris in the thirteenth century and that Thomas Aquinas set out to refute.
historical_origin: Developed by Averroes in his commentaries on Aristotle's De Anima, as his considered interpretation of Aristotle's own ambiguous remarks on nous.
examples: Russell's own judgment that the De Anima 'leads much more naturally to the view of Averroes than to that of Aquinas' (a claim made explicit in the next chapter but rooted in this one)
objections: Combated by Christian philosophers, above all Thomas Aquinas, precisely because it denies personal immortality
Regarded by orthodox Mohammedans as heretical, contributing to Averroes's own persecution and exile
competing_positions: Aquinas's view that each individual has his own immortal intellect, not a single intellect shared by all
influence_on_later_thinkers: Produced 'Averroism' as an unprofessional free-thinking movement in medieval Europe, and shaped debate especially among Franciscans and at the University of Paris in the thirteenth century.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Averroes was exiled and his books burned by order of Caliph Al-Mansur after orthodox theologians accused him of preferring 'the philosophy of the ancients' to the true faith.
